extracted.intended_audience: general public; readers interested in health, medicine, product safety, and history
extracted.subtask_short: news feature on product tampering history
extracted.subtask_description: A journalistic/historical feature recounting the 1982 Tylenol cyanide poisonings and the subsequent corporate, regulatory, and industry changes to over‑the‑counter medication safety. It explains actions taken by the company, regulators, and lawmakers and the long‑term effects on packaging and public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate mass warnings and recall
rubrics_metrics.description: McNeil/Johnson & Johnson 'took an active role with the media in issuing mass warning communications and immediately called for a massive recall of the more than 31 million bottles of Tylenol in circulation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promptly notify the public and remove potentially dangerous products from the market; large-scale recalls are an appropriate immediate response when contamination is suspected. Example: recall >31 million bottles. Scoring notes: speed and comprehensiveness of the recall are key measures of effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active engagement with media and authoritative communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The company 'took an active role with the media in issuing mass warning communications' and responded 'swiftly and authoritatively.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicate openly, frequently, and authoritatively through media channels to inform consumers and limit panic. Transparency and clarity are critical to maintaining or restoring public trust. Anti-pattern: evasive or minimal communication that leaves the public uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer replacements and incentives to affected consumers
rubrics_metrics.description: Johnson & Johnson 'offered replacement capsules to those who turned in pills already purchased and a reward for anyone with information leading to the apprehension of the individual or people involved.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide tangible remediation (product replacement, refunds) and incentives (rewards for information) to assist consumers and encourage cooperation with investigations. Such steps help demonstrate corporate responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce tamper‑proof packaging with visible tamper indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: They 'introduced a new tamper-proof packaging, which included foil seals and other features that made it obvious to a consumer if foul play had transpired.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design packaging so tampering is evident (foil seals, seals that must be broken, visible indicators). Industry adoption of such features is a desired standard. Examples: foil seals and other obvious tamper indicators; became industry standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product redesign to reduce tampering vulnerability (caplet)
rubrics_metrics.description: The company introduced a new version of their pills called the 'caplet' — 'a tablet coated with slick, easy-to-swallow gelatin but far harder to tamper with than the older capsules.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When feasible, redesign product form to reduce ease of tampering while maintaining consumer usability. Evaluate tradeoffs between convenience (e.g., easy‑to‑swallow capsules) and security (more tamper‑resistant tablets/caplets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Work collaboratively with regulators (FDA) to implement safety measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Working with FDA officials, they introduced new tamper‑proof packaging and other protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate with regulatory agencies to develop and deploy safety standards and packaging requirements. Collaboration ensures technical feasibility and regulatory compliance; is a key part of an effective response strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative and regulatory response as part of prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1983 Congress passed the 'Tylenol bill,' making it a federal offense to tamper with consumer products; in 1989 the FDA 'established federal guidelines for manufacturers to make all such products tamper-proof.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long‑term prevention can require legislation and formal regulatory guidelines that criminalize tampering and mandate safety standards. Evaluate success by whether laws/regulations reduce incidents and standardize industry practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial investment to rebuild brand trust and safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Within a year, after 'an investment of more than $100 million, Tylenol's sales rebounded' and the brand recovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to invest significant resources (financial, logistical, communications) to implement safety fixes and rebuild consumer confidence. Measure success by market recovery and consumer trust metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid investigation and product tracing to identify contamination sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators 'made the connection between the poisoning deaths and Tylenol' and hypothesized that 'someone...must have taken bottles off the shelves...laced the capsules...and then returned the restored packages to the shelves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct fast, thorough forensic and epidemiological investigations to link illnesses to products, trace distribution points, and identify tampering vectors (shelf removal/return, supply chain vulnerabilities). Removing discovered tainted inventory and tracing origins are essential actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design consideration: balance user convenience against tamper risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The gelatin-based capsules 'were especially popular because they were slick and easy to swallow' but could be 'easily opened, laced with a contaminant, and then placed back in the older non-tamper-proof bottle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing OTC products, weigh consumer convenience (ease of swallowing) against security (difficulty of tampering). Recognize that certain forms (e.g., loose capsules) may present higher tampering risks and require compensating packaging or redesign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent editorial correction of factual errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Editor's note: 'This report has been updated to remove the reported amount of cyanide used.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting errors are identified, update content transparently and note corrections or updates publicly. This maintains journalistic credibility and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis management judged by speed, authority, and consumer protections
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The dire situation...made it imperative that the Johnson & Johnson executives respond swiftly and authoritatively.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective crisis management should be rapid, authoritative, prioritize consumer safety, and include concrete protective measures (recalls, packaging changes, refunds). Evaluations should consider timeliness, decisiveness, and consumer-centered actions.
